title: Why data structures + Big O basics
syllabusDesc: See how structure choice changes speed and memory, and read Big O at a glance.
inlineSample:
items = [1, 2, 3]
print(3 in items)  # O(n) scan

counts = {"a": 2, "b": 1}
print(counts.get("a", 0))  # O(1) average lookup
desc:
Data structures decide how data is laid out in memory and what each operation costs. Big O notation gives a rough feel for how work grows as inputs get larger.

Pick the simplest structure that keeps your critical operations cheap.
placeholder:
# Try measuring rough runtime differences
import time

numbers = list(range(10000))
start = time.time()
for _ in range(1000):
    9999 in numbers
print("list membership took", time.time() - start)
solution:
import time

# Compare membership on list vs set
numbers = list(range(10000))
nums_set = set(numbers)

start = time.time()
for _ in range(1000):
    9999 in numbers
print("list membership took", round(time.time() - start, 4), "seconds")

start = time.time()
for _ in range(1000):
    9999 in nums_set
print("set membership took", round(time.time() - start, 4), "seconds")

print("Big O takeaway: list membership ~O(n); set/dict membership ~O(1) average.")
techniques: Estimate time vs space costs with Big O notation
Favor the simplest structure that keeps critical operations fast
Translate requirements (fast lookup? ordered iteration?) into structure choice
challenges: List 3 daily-life examples of when you need fast lookup vs fast ordering
Show an O(n) vs O(1) difference for membership using a larger input size
Explain why a sorted list might beat a hash table for small data
notes:
Big O is a growth rate, not a stopwatch. Constant factors matter for small inputs.

Prefer readability first; optimize when you know which operation matters most.
